title: Your fastest nerve fibres carry signals at over 100 m/s; your slowest, under 1 m/s
body: Nerve signals are not all equally quick. Conduction speeds in the human body range from about **0.5 m/s to more than 120 m/s**, depending mostly on two things: how thick the axon is and whether it is wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating sheath that lets the impulse jump between gaps. The thick, myelinated sensory fibres that report muscle stretch run at 80 to 120 m/s, while thin, unmyelinated C fibres creep along at 0.5 to 2 m/s. Temperature matters too: cold slows nerve conduction and warmth speeds it up.

cover.alt: A confocal microscope image of cultured rat hippocampal neurons, their axons glowing orange and gold in a dense web against black

slides.heading: Rank these nerve fibres by top speed
slides.note: Top of each fibre type's range
slides.explanation: Thick, heavily myelinated fibres are fastest. Ia sensory fibres reach 80–120 m/s, motor Aα fibres 50–60, Aβ 33–75, Aδ 3–30, and C fibres only 0.5–2 m/s.

slides.heading: Why myelin makes the difference
slides.text: Myelin wraps an axon in insulating segments with tiny gaps between them. Instead of regenerating the impulse along every bit of membrane, a myelinated fibre lets it leap from gap to gap, a process called saltatory conduction. Add a wide axon, which offers less resistance, and the signal races.

slides.heading: How a signal jumps along a myelinated axon

steps.label: An impulse starts at the axon's base
Myelin insulates a stretch of the axon
At a gap, the membrane fires again
The impulse leaps from gap to gap

slides.question: What happens to nerve conduction speed when a limb gets cold?
slides.explanation: Conduction velocity rises roughly linearly with temperature, so cold slows signals and warmth speeds them up.

slides.label: the range of nerve conduction speeds in the human body
slides.text: The fastest signals would cover the length of a football pitch in under a second; the slowest would take a few minutes.
